concept.body: Hinge Theorem in one line: same two sides, the BIGGER included angle makes the LONGER third side (like opening a door wider). Its converse runs backward: the LONGER third side came from the BIGGER included angle. Equal included angles give SAS congruence (equal third sides).

explanationVariants: A bigger included angle produces a longer third side.
Wider hinge → wider gap → longer third side.

widget.prompt: Two triangles share two side lengths. The one with the bigger included angle has the…

options.label: longer third side
options.feedback: Opening the included angle wider stretches the third side longer.

options.label: shorter third side
options.feedback: That's backward — a bigger angle makes a LONGER third side, not shorter.

options.label: same third side
options.feedback: Same third side needs equal angles (SAS). A bigger angle gives a longer third side.

options.label: smaller area only
options.feedback: A wider angle up to 90° actually increases area; regardless, the third side gets LONGER.

steps.body: Picture a door hinge with two fixed arms. Open it wider and the gap between the arm-ends grows. That's the **Hinge Theorem**: if two triangles share two pairs of equal sides, the one with the **larger included angle** has the **longer third side**. Same two sides, bigger angle, bigger opposite side.

widget.prompt: Two triangles both have sides 7 and 5. Triangle P's included angle is 40°; triangle Q's is 80°. Which has the longer third side?

options.label: Triangle Q (the 80° angle)
options.feedback: The larger included angle opens the third side wider — Q's 80° beats P's 40°, so Q's third side is longer.

options.label: Triangle P (the 40° angle)
options.feedback: A smaller angle makes a SHORTER third side. The wider 80° angle (Q) gives the longer side.

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Equal only if the angles were equal — but 40° ≠ 80°, so the third sides differ. Q's is longer.

options.label: It depends on the side lengths
options.feedback: Both share the SAME two sides (7 and 5), so only the angle matters — the bigger angle (Q) wins.

explanationVariants: With the two sides fixed, widening the included angle swings their endpoints apart, stretching the third side.
The included angle acts like a hinge: open it more and the gap (third side) grows.

widget.prompt: In the hinge theorem, what causes the third side to lengthen?

options.label: Widening the included angle swings the two fixed sides' endpoints farther apart
options.feedback: The two sides stay the same length; opening the angle between them increases the distance across — a longer third side.

options.label: The two given sides get longer
options.feedback: The two sides are FIXED and equal in both triangles — only the ANGLE changes. That's what moves the third side.

options.label: The triangle's area stays constant
options.feedback: Area actually changes as the angle opens, but the KEY driver of the third side is the widening angle itself.

options.label: The third side is always the longest
options.feedback: The third side needn't be longest — the point is it GROWS as the included angle widens.

steps.body: The Hinge Theorem is really the **SAS inequality** — a cousin of SAS congruence. SAS congruence: equal sides AND equal included angle ⇒ equal third sides (congruent). The hinge: equal sides but a BIGGER included angle ⇒ a bigger third side. Equal angle gives equal; bigger angle gives bigger.

widget.prompt: Two triangles have two pairs of equal sides. If their included angles are also EQUAL, what follows?

options.label: The triangles are congruent (SAS), so the third sides are equal
options.feedback: Equal sides plus equal included angle is SAS congruence — the third sides match exactly.

options.label: The third sides differ by the hinge theorem
options.feedback: The hinge applies when the angles DIFFER. Equal included angles give SAS congruence and equal third sides.

options.label: Nothing can be concluded
options.feedback: Equal sides and equal included angle is precisely SAS — a strong conclusion: congruent triangles.

options.label: The triangles are only similar
options.feedback: SAS gives full congruence (same size), not mere similarity, when the included angles are equal.

explanationVariants: The converse: with two equal side-pairs, the triangle with the LONGER third side has the LARGER included angle.
Run the hinge backward — a bigger third side implies a bigger included angle.

widget.prompt: Two triangles share two pairs of equal sides. Triangle P's third side is longer than Q's. What does the CONVERSE hinge theorem conclude?

options.label: P's included angle is larger than Q's
options.feedback: The converse runs backward: a longer third side means a wider included angle. P's angle is larger.

options.label: P's included angle is smaller than Q's
options.feedback: A longer third side comes from a WIDER angle, not a narrower one — P's angle is larger, not smaller.

options.label: Their included angles are equal
options.feedback: Equal angles would give equal third sides (SAS). Since P's third side is longer, its angle is larger.

options.label: P is congruent to Q
options.feedback: Different third sides rule out congruence. The converse says P's included angle is the larger one.

steps.body: A neat door analogy seals it: the two door edges are the fixed sides; the hinge is the included angle; the gap you'd measure between the door's free edge and the frame is the third side. Swing the door open wider, the gap widens. Close it, the gap shrinks toward zero.

predict.prompt: Two sides stay fixed and only the angle between them grows. Does the third side ALWAYS grow too?

options.label: Always — a bigger included angle means a bigger opposite side, no exceptions
Sometimes — it depends on which two sides are fixed
No — the third side can shrink even as the angle grows

predict.reveal: Always. Drag the included angle open and watch the third side's length climb without ever turning back — a hinge swinging wider always pushes its far ends further apart. That one-way relationship is the whole hinge theorem.

widget.prompt: Sides 5 and 8 are fixed. Open the included angle and watch the third side — does it ever shrink as the angle grows?
widget.successFeedback: At 60° the third side reaches exactly 7 — right between its length at 30° (about 4.4) and at 120° (about 11.4). Every larger angle gave a larger side, in that order, with no exceptions: that monotonic climb IS the hinge theorem.
widget.lowFeedback: Still short of 7 — open the angle further and watch the third side keep climbing, never falling back.
widget.highFeedback: Past 7 now — ease the angle back and watch the third side shrink, but only because the angle did.

hints: Both triangles have sides 6 and 9. Compare their included angles.
The triangle with the larger included angle has the longer third side.
50° < 70°, so the 70° triangle has the longer third side.
explanationVariants: Same two sides (6 and 9); the larger included angle (70° > 50°) gives the longer third side — the 70° triangle.
By the hinge, bigger included angle → longer third side: the 70° triangle wins.

widget.prompt: Triangle X has sides 6 and 9 with a 50° included angle. Triangle Y has sides 6 and 9 with a 70° included angle. Which third side is longer?

options.label: Triangle Y's (70° included angle)
options.feedback: Same two sides, larger included angle (70° > 50°) — Y's third side is longer by the hinge theorem.

options.label: Triangle X's (50° included angle)
options.feedback: The smaller angle makes the SHORTER third side. Y's wider 70° angle gives the longer one.

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Equal only if the included angles matched — but 50° ≠ 70°, so Y's third side is longer.

options.label: Cannot be determined
options.feedback: It can: the sides are identical, so the larger included angle (Y) determines the longer third side.

takeaways: Hinge Theorem: equal two sides, larger included angle ⇒ longer third side.
It's the SAS inequality — equal angle gives equal (SAS congruence), bigger angle gives bigger.
Converse: longer third side ⇒ larger included angle.
